variants.name: Blocking attempt loop with std::this_thread::sleep_for
variants.implementation_notes: C++ ships no retry facility, so the schedule is a hand-written loop: compute delay = min(cap, base * 2^(attempt-1)), draw the jittered delay from a std::uniform_real_distribution (full jitter), then std::this_thread::sleep_for. The standard requires sleep_for to block for at least the requested duration and recommends measuring that duration with a steady clock, so keep the total budget on std::chrono::steady_clock. The classic blocking form is still justified whenever the calling thread is dedicated to the operation and cancellation is not required; in an io_context-driven service, prefer the timer variant so the wait does not consume a thread.
pitfalls: sleep_for may oversleep (scheduling, resource contention) and a wall-clock budget can drift; measure the total budget on std::chrono::steady_clock.
A thread parked in sleep_for cannot be interrupted, so shutdown and caller deadlines wait out the full delay; use the timer variant or a condition_variable when cancellation matters.
Seeding a std::mt19937 from the clock inside the call re-synchronizes concurrent callers; keep one generator per thread (thread_local) or pass one in.

variants.name: Boost.Asio steady_timer / C++20 coroutine wait
variants.implementation_notes: When the operation already runs on an io_context, the backoff should be a timer event rather than a blocked thread: a boost::asio::steady_timer with expires_after(delay) and async_wait (or co_await with C++20 stackless coroutines) schedules the next attempt while releasing the thread, and the steady_timer typedef selects the steady clock that must measure the delay anyway. Cancellation is explicit: changing the expiry of a pending async_wait cancels it and the handler completes with operation_aborted, which is how a caller deadline or object destruction aborts the retry loop. Choose this variant in event-loop services where a sleeping thread per pending retry would exhaust the pool.
pitfalls: The timer and the operation must share one executor; awaiting a timer on a different context deadlocks or races.
A cancelled async_wait completes with operation_aborted, which must not be mistaken for a dependency failure and retried.
Detached co_spawn erases ownership: the retry coroutine must own its state, or the timer and the operation outlive the objects they touch.
